strengths: Compelling and practically motivated setup: leveraging routine interactive clicks from clinical workflows to drive online test-time adaptation addresses the realistic problem of deployment distribution shifts without requiring explicit manual ground-truth re-annotation.

Computationally efficient adaptation pipeline: the proposed two-stage optimization requires only two backpropagation steps per image, presenting a notable efficiency advantage over prior online adaptation methods such as TSCA (10 backprops) and IA+SA.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse domain shifts: evaluated on 5 retinal fundus datasets (multi-class disc/cup) and 4 brain MRI datasets covering cross-scanner, cross-modality (FLAIR to T1, T1c, T2), and cross-pathology shifts.

Informative ablation studies: the experiments in Figure 3 clearly justify the distinct roles of Stage 1 (localization), Stage 2 (correction responsiveness), and the Gaussian Point Loss (GPL) in stabilizing continual updates.
weaknesses: Dependence on simulated user interactions: click interactions are generated deterministically via synthetic heuristics (connected-component error regions). In real clinical practice, clinician clicks are often noisy, clustered, or suboptimal; the paper lacks evaluation or robustness analysis under noisy or non-ideal user behavior.

Risk of error propagation and drift: adaptation relies entirely on pseudo ground truth generated by the base model with clicks. Although Figure 3 (bottom) monitors a held-out set over hundreds of images, there is limited formal analysis of model drift, catastrophic forgetting of source domains, or failure cases when pseudo-labels contain persistent errors.

Backbone choice and generalizability: the adaptation method is only applied to an older CNN-based model (ISFCNN). Demonstrating compatibility with modern transformer-based interactive segmentation architectures (such as MedSAM or SAM) would significantly strengthen the impact and relevance of the framework.

Limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: several task-specific hyperparameters (e.g., Gaussian window cutoff of 10, kernel standard deviation sigma=3, and weight beta=200) are introduced without ablation or sensitivity discussion across varying image resolutions.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated setting: Continually adapting interactive medical image segmentation models from post-deployment user feedback is clinically relevant and addresses the critical problem of domain shift.

Efficient adaptation design: Compared to existing continual interactive methods (e.g., TSCA, IA+SA) that require gradient updates at each interactive click (10+ backpropagation passes per image), the proposed two-stage scheme performs only two backward passes per sample while achieving better performance.

Well-designed technical components: The Gaussian Point Loss (GPL) effectively regularizes the spatial neighborhood of correction clicks, and the two-stage formulation cleanly decouples initial target localization (Stage 1) from multi-point error correction (Stage 2).

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments cover 5 fundus datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets across multiple shift scenarios, including cross-center, cross-modality (FLAIR to T1/T1c/T2), and cross-pathology shifts (glioma to stroke and traumatic brain injury).

Informative ablation studies: The ablations convincingly validate the individual contributions of Stage 1, Stage 2, and the GPL loss, as well as the adaptation stability across a sequence of incoming images.
weaknesses: Synthetic interaction vs. real clinical workflows: The evaluation relies entirely on simulated click sequences derived from ground-truth error masks. In practice, clinician interactions can be sub-optimal or noisy, and the pseudo-ground truth generated after T clicks may contain systematic residual errors.

Reliance on older backbone architecture: The adaptation strategy is implemented on ISFCNN (a standard 2D U-Net). While MedSAM Adapter is included as a baseline, showing whether the proposed online adaptation strategy directly generalizes to modern prompt-based foundation models (e.g., MedSAM or SAM) would substantially increase impact.

Analysis of long-term stability and catastrophic drift: Continuous online learning without replay buffers or parameter regularizers risks distribution drift over long, non-stationary sequences. An explicit analysis on order sensitivity or long-term retention of source domain capability would strengthen the paper.
Minor presentation issues: The running headers in the manuscript read 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length', which should be fixed with a short title.

strengths: Practical and clinically relevant problem formulation: adapting interactive segmentation models continuously during inference using clinical feedback addresses a major barrier in medical image deployment under domain shifts.

Computational efficiency during test-time adaptation: the two-stage procedure requires only two backward passes per image, in contrast to existing continual interactive methods (e.g., TSCA, IA+SA) which require 10 or more backward passes.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shift scenarios, covering 5 fundus imaging datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets spanning cross-scanner, cross-modality, and cross-pathology shifts.
Solid empirical performance gains over relevant online adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) as well as static models across varying click counts (1, 5, 10).
Informative ablation studies illustrating the individual contributions of Stage 1, Stage 2, and the Gaussian Point Loss (GPL) along both interaction iterations and long adaptation sequences.
weaknesses: Simplistic evaluation on 3D volumetric MRI: 3D MRI volumes (BraTS, ATLAS, WMH) are reduced to a single 2D slice with the largest lesion per subject. This simplifies the clinical task significantly and overlooks volumetric spatial continuity and inter-slice variations central to 3D medical segmentation.

Lack of human reader evaluation: All adaptation and evaluation procedures rely strictly on automated heuristic click simulation (connected component centroids/random sampling). Human clinicians often click unpredictably, near boundaries, or make suboptimal selections, which may introduce severe confirmation bias and error propagation during pseudo-labeling.

Incomplete metric reporting: The paper evaluates solely on Dice score. Standard interactive segmentation benchmarks typically report Number of Clicks (NoC@85 / NoC@90) to measure interactive efficiency, along with boundary distance metrics such as 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) or Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD).

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The proposed approach fundamentally combines standard pseudo-label self-training (using the multi-click output as the target) with a Gaussian-weighted neighborhood loss around simulated clicks.

Potential vulnerability to error accumulation: Relying on the base model's prediction after $T$ clicks as the pseudo ground truth in Stage 1 carries a risk of confirmation bias under severe distribution shifts where $T$ clicks are insufficient to correct severe errors; a more formal safeguard against catastrophic drift across long sequences is lacking.

Sensitivity and scale dependency of hyperparameters: The Gaussian Point Loss uses a fixed spatial window (|i'-i| <= 10) and variance (sigma = 3), which are sensitive to image resolution and lesion size, yet no sensitivity analysis or multi-scale adaptation is provided.

strengths: Practical and well-formulated motivation: Leveraging interactive human-in-the-loop corrections to perform online adaptation under distribution shift is highly relevant for clinical deployment.

Sound methodological design: The combination of Mid-Interaction (MI) adaptation, two-stage Post-Interaction (PI) adaptation with synthetic correction clicks, and the Click-Centered Gaussian (CCG) loss effectively addresses the spatial sparsity issue inherent in prior point-based online adaptation methods (e.g., TSCA, IA+SA).

Extensive and convincing empirical validation: Tested across 5 retinal fundus datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets spanning multiple modalities and pathologies, demonstrating consistent and substantial gains (e.g., >10% Dice improvement in difficult MRI transfer scenarios).

Thorough ablation and robustness analysis: The paper includes rigorous evaluations exploring click budgets (3, 5, 10, 50 clicks), hyperparameter sensitivities (alpha, beta, sigma), robustness to noisy/erroneous clicks, extreme domain shifts, shuffled multi-domain streams, and computational latency.
weaknesses: Simplified 2D evaluation on inherently 3D volumetric data: For 3D brain MRI benchmarks (BraTS, ATLAS, WMH, TBI), the evaluation is restricted to 2D slices by picking the slice with the largest lesion area. Validating the approach on full 3D volumes would strengthen clinical relevance.

Reliance on simulated user interactions: All evaluations are conducted using heuristic simulated clicks. While this is standard practice in interactive segmentation literature, validation with real clinical annotators is missing.

Full-network online updating: Updating all parameters online after each click could be computationally demanding for larger backbones or 3D architectures; exploring parameter-efficient adaptation (e.g., LoRA or lightweight adapters) would be a valuable addition.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated framework: Leveraging interactive user corrections not just for momentary mask refinement but for continuous online test-time adaptation directly addresses real-world clinical deployment challenges under domain shift.

Sensible and effective technical components: The two-stage Post-Interaction adaptation (using the refined prediction as pseudo ground-truth) paired with Mid-Interaction updates and the Click-Centered Gaussian (CCG) loss provides an intuitive, lean, and regularizer-free approach that effectively focuses gradient updates near corrected regions.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across diverse medical imaging domains (5 fundus datasets and 4 brain MRI lesion datasets across multiple modalities and pathologies), demonstrating consistent and substantial improvements (often >10% Dice) over competitive online adaptation baselines such as IA+SA and TSCA.

Thorough ablations and robustness analysis: The paper includes extensive ablation studies of each loss component and hyperparameter, evaluations under restricted click budgets (3, 5 clicks), run-time latency benchmarks (sub-second on both GPU and CPU), and robustness stress-tests (mixed-dataset sequences, worst-first ordering, and up to 40% erroneous clicks).
weaknesses: Reliance on simulated user interactions: While automated click simulation is standard practice in interactive segmentation literature, validation with actual human-in-the-loop user studies (evaluating real clinician behavior, latency, and interaction patterns) is missing.

2D evaluation on volumetric data: For 3D MRI datasets (BraTS, ATLAS, WMH, TBI), the evaluation is performed strictly on 2D slices with the largest lesion area per volume. Testing on full 3D interactive workflows or multi-slice volumetric contexts would better reflect clinical reality.

Limited exploration of modern foundation model backbones: Although the computational argument for using a lightweight U-Net is sensible for real-time online updates, comparing primarily against a frozen Med-SA leaves open the question of how this adaptation framework performs when applied to adapter layers of vision foundation models (e.g., SAM).

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem formulation: adapting interactive segmentation models online to real-time clinical distribution shifts without requiring offline retraining or manual ground-truth masks.
Extensive and thorough experimental validation spanning 5 fundus imaging datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets (covering cross-modality and cross-pathology shifts).

Comprehensive robustness and ablation analyses, including tests against extreme domain shifts, adversarial image ordering ('worst case first'), noisy user clicks, hyperparameter sensitivity, and latency benchmarks demonstrating real-time feasibility.

Strong empirical gains over relevant interactive online adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) and non-adapting models, with particularly dramatic improvements in severe shift scenarios (e.g., BRATS FLAIR to T1).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: the core framework builds upon known paradigms of online adaptation from user clicks and pseudo-labeling, with the primary technical innovations being the Click-Centered Gaussian (CCG) weighting and a multi-stage post/mid-interaction update schedule.

Evaluation on 3D MRI scans is simplified to single 2D slices (the largest lesion slice per case), which omits volumetric context, 3D propagation, and practical slice-to-slice interactive workflows typical in clinical neuroimaging.

Reliance entirely on simulated click heuristics: although standard in the interactive segmentation literature, the lack of a real user/clinician study leaves open questions about how the adaptation behaves under genuine, non-ideal human interaction patterns.

The Mid-Interaction loss formulation (optimizing the discrepancy between $P_{t-1}$ and $P_t^{initial}$) is somewhat heuristic and would benefit from deeper theoretical analysis or formal justification regarding gradient dynamics and stability.
